operationalization: Fit longitudinal length or mass trajectories with and without an annually periodic term whose amplitude declines with age, separately in plaice, haddock, and humans. Support requires improved out-of-sample fit and declining seasonal amplitude in each stated group.

candidate_datasets.name: International Council for the Exploration of the Sea Data Centre
candidate_datasets.role: Public fisheries survey data can provide repeated size-at-age observations for plaice and haddock.

candidate_datasets.name: FishBase
candidate_datasets.role: Growth parameters and life-history records can identify relevant species and growth series.

obstacles: Cross-sectional fish surveys do not track the same individuals.
Open human longitudinal records with fine seasonal resolution are limited.
rationale: Seasonality and damping have direct statistical meanings and can be compared with nonperiodic growth models. Existing fish data can test population-level patterns, but the full claim needs longitudinal, seasonally resolved measurements in both fishes and humans.

operationalization: Construct Arizona ponderosa-pine ring-width chronologies for the stated interval, remove age trends, and test for a stable approximately 150-year spectral peak against red-noise and nonstationary alternatives. Compare the chronology with independent moisture and temperature reconstructions to identify the climatic correlate.

candidate_datasets.name: NOAA International Tree-Ring Data Bank
candidate_datasets.role: Open ring-width chronologies and measurements from Arizona ponderosa pine support direct reanalysis.

candidate_datasets.name: NOAA Paleoclimatology Data
candidate_datasets.role: Independent hydroclimate and temperature reconstructions allow comparison of candidate climatic drivers.

obstacles: Only about three cycles occur in a 500-year window.
Detrending and smoothing choices can create or suppress low-frequency peaks.
rationale: The period, location, proxy, and time window define a direct test. Public tree-ring archives have the necessary raw measurements and long chronology, while modern spectral methods can quantify uncertainty and distinguish periodicity from autocorrelated variability.

operationalization: Relate cell-volume or organ elongation rates to water uptake, turgor, osmotic potential, and metabolic rate, then estimate the variance or causal response attributable to water status. The claim is supported where perturbations or time series show growth rate tracking water uptake after metabolic covariates are controlled.

candidate_datasets.name: TRY Plant Trait Database
candidate_datasets.role: Plant hydraulic and growth traits can support broad but indirect tests of water-status associations.

candidate_datasets.name: Dryad
candidate_datasets.role: Hosts public experimental datasets on plant growth, water potential, and osmotic treatments that could be compiled.

obstacles: The phrase 'in great measure' lacks a quantitative threshold.
Matched water-uptake, metabolism, and growth measurements are scattered.
Animal and plant mechanisms differ substantially.
rationale: The variables are measurable, but the stated breadth and vague effect size require interpretation. Existing experiments can test subsets, especially plant elongation, but no unified public dataset appears adequate for growing cells across plants and animals.

operationalization: Measure abdomen-to-cephalothorax length in Artemia raised or sampled across salinity gradients and fit the ratio as a function of salinity while controlling species, sex, age, and population. A consistently positive salinity effect supports the claim; no effect or a negative effect refutes it.

candidate_datasets.name: Dryad
candidate_datasets.role: Public Artemia salinity experiments and morphometric supplements may provide measurements for a compiled test.

candidate_datasets.name: Zenodo
candidate_datasets.role: Open experimental and imaging datasets can supplement Artemia morphology-by-salinity records.

obstacles: Morphometric data paired with exact salinity are scattered.
Genetic differentiation and age can confound environmental plasticity.
rationale: The predictor, response ratio, and direction are explicit and experimentally discriminating. Public data likely cover some strains and salinities, but a broad species-level test would require harmonizing multiple studies.

operationalization: Fit organismal growth time series with an explicit autocatalytic-reaction velocity model and compare predictive fit against logistic, Gompertz, von Bertalanffy, and flexible spline alternatives. The resemblance is supported only if the autocatalytic shape consistently captures the stated acceleration and retardation phases without being outperformed.

candidate_datasets.name: FishBase
candidate_datasets.role: Provides extensive species-level growth parameters and observations for testing common growth-curve shapes.

candidate_datasets.name: TRY Plant Trait Database
candidate_datasets.role: Plant growth and life-history traits provide data for a restricted taxonomic test.

obstacles: 'Closely resembles' has no specified goodness-of-fit threshold.
Many unrelated growth models yield similar sigmoid curves.
Available databases often store fitted parameters rather than raw time series.
rationale: Growth curves are abundant and model comparison is straightforward, but qualitative resemblance has weak discriminating power. Existing data can resolve the pattern in selected taxa, not the claim's organism-wide scope.

operationalization: Compare growth rate, final size, and body-part proportions between hormone or iodine perturbations and matched controls. Support requires accelerated growth accompanied by a statistically detectable allometric or shape change, not size alone.

candidate_datasets.name: Gene Expression Omnibus
candidate_datasets.role: Public hormone-perturbation studies often include treatment metadata and developmental phenotypes.

candidate_datasets.name: Dryad
candidate_datasets.role: Hosts open endocrine and developmental experiments with growth and morphology measurements.

candidate_datasets.name: Image Data Resource
candidate_datasets.role: Public biological imaging datasets can provide morphology under defined perturbations.

obstacles: Phenotype measurements and treatment doses are heterogeneous.
The claim combines many substances and animal groups.
rationale: Controlled perturbations make the causal statement directly testable, and many relevant studies have public data. Coverage is nevertheless uneven, so existing datasets can establish examples rather than fully resolve the broad generalization.

operationalization: Define origination as the appearance of phenotypic variants through developmental change and removal as differential extinction or reproductive loss, then compare the timing of variation with subsequent selection in fossil and population time series. Evidence that variants predate selective sorting supports the restricted proposition, while the universal claim would require this sequence across evolutionary transitions.

candidate_datasets.name: Paleobiology Database
candidate_datasets.role: Open fossil occurrence data can test whether disappearance patterns align with selective removal in documented clades.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoBank
candidate_datasets.role: Public morphological matrices can characterize form appearance and loss in selected phylogenetic histories.

obstacles: Origination and removal are partly conceptual categories.
Fossil sampling obscures the timing and causes of appearance and disappearance.
Universal scope cannot be established from available cases.
rationale: A restricted temporal prediction can be tested, but Thompson's universal division of causal roles is underspecified and difficult to distinguish from standard views in which selection changes variant frequencies. Existing macroevolutionary data address examples, not the universal assertion.

operationalization: Derive regenerative tail length or volume velocity from time-lapse measurements after its early maximum and fit a power law V proportional to T raised to negative alpha. The claim is supported if alpha is near 2 and V times T squared is approximately constant, compared with alternative decay models.

candidate_datasets.name: BioImage Archive
candidate_datasets.role: Public developmental imaging studies may contain time-resolved tadpole tail-regeneration series.

candidate_datasets.name: Dryad
candidate_datasets.role: Hosts regeneration-study measurements and image supplements suitable for reanalysis.

obstacles: Few public series have dense enough time sampling to estimate velocity.
Species, temperature, and injury extent affect the exponent.
rationale: This is a precise quantitative law with strong discrimination among decay models. Data exist for regeneration, but the exact historical scope and sufficiently dense tadpole trajectories are not guaranteed in a single open dataset.

operationalization: Normalize complete regeneration and whole-organism growth trajectories and compare their latent, accelerating, peak-velocity, and decelerating phases using shared versus separate curve families. Support requires a common curve structure across matched tissues or taxa; systematic phase or shape differences refute it.

candidate_datasets.name: BioImage Archive
candidate_datasets.role: Time-lapse regeneration and development images can yield comparable growth trajectories.

candidate_datasets.name: Dryad
candidate_datasets.role: Open regeneration and ontogenetic-growth datasets can be assembled for model comparison.

obstacles: 'Same essential characteristics' permits multiple interpretations.
Matched regeneration and zero-origin ontogeny data are rare.
Normalization can conceal biologically important differences.
rationale: Curve features can be quantified, but the asserted equivalence is qualitative and spans unlike processes. Existing data permit comparisons in selected systems, not a decisive general test.

operationalization: For individually tracked asymmetric-clawed crustaceans, estimate post-amputation growth rates of both claws and test whether their ratio predicts retention versus reversal of claw identity and morphology. A threshold relationship that predicts outcomes independently of species and body size would support the mechanism.

candidate_datasets.name: Dryad
candidate_datasets.role: May contain public crustacean regeneration experiments, though matched bilateral time series are sparse.

obstacles: The required individual-level bilateral growth trajectories are rarely archived.
Neural and positional effects could confound a rate-only explanation.
rationale: The proposed rate ratio and fate outcome make a clear prospective test. Public literature documents claw regeneration, but the paired longitudinal variables needed to adjudicate this mechanism appear insufficient.

operationalization: Quantify spontaneous break locations and stresses in living worm-like animals, then test whether physical instability of a long semifluid tube predicts fission across taxa after accounting for active cellular patterning; separately verify regeneration of missing parts. Refutation would be patterned fission preceding mechanical instability or requiring specific molecular programs absent from nonfissioning relatives.
obstacles: Mechanical state at the instant of fission is not represented in broad public datasets.
The proposed physical tendency lacks a unique quantitative model.
Comparative occurrence alone cannot distinguish passive breakage from regulated development.
rationale: The regeneration component is measurable, but the claimed essential physical cause needs synchronized mechanics and molecular observations. Existing comparative and imaging records are too incomplete to discriminate passive instability from active fission programs.

operationalization: Synchronously measure growth velocity, surface stiffness or skin formation, and internal growth-driving pressure through the velocity peak. Support requires the velocity break to follow an abrupt resistance increase while internal drive remains stable; a preceding drop in drive would favor the rival.

candidate_datasets.name: BioImage Archive
candidate_datasets.role: Time-lapse developmental imaging can locate growth transitions, but usually lacks simultaneous force measurements.

obstacles: Existing images rarely include surface resistance and internal driving force.
The claim spans organisms with different growth mechanics.
Histological differentiation and slowing are temporally correlated confounders.
rationale: The rival mechanisms imply different synchronized trajectories, so the claim is testable in principle. However, current public datasets generally do not combine mechanics, histology, and growth at the required temporal resolution.

operationalization: Represent ontogenetic and phylogenetic shape changes in a common morphometric space and compare their trajectories, directions, and ordering of landmarks. Support requires phylogenetic transformations to follow the same paths as within-individual development more often than null or alternative developmental models predict.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: Open 3D specimens across ages and species support shared-space geometric morphometrics.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoBank
candidate_datasets.role: Public morphological matrices and images can link comparative form with phylogeny.

obstacles: Ancestral forms must be inferred rather than observed.
Heterochrony can mimic shared paths.
The universal 'one road' formulation is much broader than available clade datasets.
rationale: Modern geometric morphometrics gives the claim measurable trajectory predictions. Public specimens allow strong tests in selected clades, but ancestral inference and limited ontogenetic series prevent resolving the universal statement.

operationalization: No non-arbitrary dataset analysis can assign 'little value' to structure or separate material structures from the forces embodied by them without first choosing a philosophical definition of explanatory value.
obstacles: 'Value' is normative.
Structure and dynamics are not mutually exclusive causal categories.
rationale: Although modern imaging links cell structures to dynamics, the claim primarily ranks explanatory programs rather than specifying a measurable consequence. Any result could be redescribed as structure expressing forces, so it does not cleanly discriminate rivals.

operationalization: Use live-cell spindle imaging and perturbation data to test whether spindle fibers transmit mechanical traction and whether a distinct magnetism-like bipolar field is needed to predict chromosome and particle motion. Evidence of tensile microtubule forces sufficient to explain the pattern refutes the exclusion of mechanical traction.

candidate_datasets.name: Image Data Resource
candidate_datasets.role: Open high-content mitosis images and perturbation screens permit tests of spindle structure and mechanics.

candidate_datasets.name: BioImage Archive
candidate_datasets.role: Public live-cell microscopy provides spindle and chromosome trajectories under perturbation.

obstacles: The proposed field is analogical rather than quantitatively specified.
Images alone may not directly measure force.
rationale: The categorical rejection of traction has clear observable consequences, and open perturbation microscopy can test whether microtubule mechanics account for spindle behavior. The unspecified nature of the alternative polarizing field lowers operationalizability but does not prevent refuting the claim.

operationalization: Measure nuclear sphericity, cytoplasmic rheology, external stress anisotropy, and nuclear-envelope tension across cell types and perturbations. Support requires round nuclei in fluid isotropic surroundings and predictable deformation as surrounding stiffness or pressure anisotropy increases.

candidate_datasets.name: Image Data Resource
candidate_datasets.role: Cell-painting and perturbation images provide large-scale nuclear shape measurements.

candidate_datasets.name: Human Protein Atlas Cell Atlas
candidate_datasets.role: Public microscopy across cell lines supports comparisons of nuclear shape and cytoskeletal context.

obstacles: Most image datasets lack matched cytoplasmic rheology or pressure.
Nuclear lamina and chromatin mechanics provide plausible alternative causes.
rationale: Shape and mechanical predictors are measurable, and extensive public cell images permit broad correlational and some perturbational tests. Full discrimination of an immiscible-drop mechanism from envelope and chromatin mechanics needs variables absent from many datasets.

operationalization: Quantify cell-axis morphology and spatial distributions of forces or tension reporters, then test whether morphological polarity predicts a corresponding polarized mechanical field across ova and epithelia. A frequent axis without force anisotropy would refute a strong reading.

candidate_datasets.name: BioImage Archive
candidate_datasets.role: Public polarity and mechanobiology microscopy can pair cell axes with molecular or tension reporters.

candidate_datasets.name: Image Data Resource
candidate_datasets.role: High-content cell images support broad quantification of morphological polarity.

obstacles: 'Distribution of forces' has several modern interpretations.
Visible filament alignment is not an independent force measurement.
Matched force reporters are limited to selected systems.
rationale: A modern mechanobiological interpretation yields testable correlations and perturbation predictions. Because the historical 'field' is underspecified and many datasets visualize structure rather than force, only restricted versions are resolvable.

operationalization: Compare live and fixed-cell images of alleged alveolar networks and test whether their geometry and dynamics match two-fluid foam predictions and vary with interfacial-tension perturbations. Persistence as membrane- or cytoskeleton-defined structures with incompatible topology would refute the foam mechanism.

candidate_datasets.name: BioImage Archive
candidate_datasets.role: Open live-cell and ultrastructural imaging can distinguish dynamic droplets or foam from fixed networks.

candidate_datasets.name: Electron Microscopy Public Image Archive
candidate_datasets.role: Public volume electron microscopy provides high-resolution intracellular topology.

obstacles: The historical structure may not map uniquely to a modern organelle.
Interfacial tensions are usually not measured alongside images.
rationale: Foam topology and response to tension are distinct from membrane and cytoskeletal alternatives. Existing imaging can reject broad versions, but exact identification of Thompson's alveoli and matched physical measurements limit complete resolution.

operationalization: Register live-cell images with the same cells or matched samples after chemical fixation and quantify appearance, disappearance, and distortion of fine networks and granules versus larger organelles. A high fraction of fixation-specific fine structures alongside preservation of larger structures supports the claim.

candidate_datasets.name: BioImage Archive
candidate_datasets.role: Public correlative live/fixed microscopy datasets allow direct artifact quantification.

candidate_datasets.name: Electron Microscopy Public Image Archive
candidate_datasets.role: Open ultrastructural datasets using varied preparation methods permit cross-method comparison.

obstacles: Precisely matched live-to-fixed cells are less common than unmatched images.
Modern fixation methods differ from those Thompson criticized.
rationale: The claim makes a direct method-comparison prediction, and public correlative imaging can distinguish pre-existing structures from fixation products. Scope across all historical reagents is imperfect, but the central empirical generalization is resolvable.

operationalization: Track chromosomes during mitosis and compare their trajectories with quantitative predictions of repulsion from a bipolar field versus motor- and microtubule-based transport. Perturbing spindle microtubules or motors should leave field-driven equatorial collection intact but disrupt a mechanical mechanism.

candidate_datasets.name: Image Data Resource
candidate_datasets.role: Open mitotic perturbation screens provide chromosome localization phenotypes.

candidate_datasets.name: BioImage Archive
candidate_datasets.role: Live-cell chromosome and spindle imaging supports trajectory analysis.

obstacles: 'Diamagnetic' is an analogy without a calibrated field variable.
Most images do not measure electromagnetic susceptibility.
rationale: Modern mitosis datasets can strongly test whether known mechanical machinery explains equatorial movement and thereby refute the claimed necessity. Direct confirmation of a diamagnetic mechanism would require physical measurements not usually present.

operationalization: Measure membrane or intracellular electrical potential spatially through successive cleavages while simultaneously imaging division timing, chromatin, and polarity; perturb voltage independently and quantify effects on division. Support requires reproducible pole differences or reversals that causally alter segmentation.

candidate_datasets.name: BioImage Archive
candidate_datasets.role: Some voltage-reporter and embryogenesis imaging is public, but matched successive-cleavage datasets are limited.

obstacles: Historical 'potential' does not map uniquely to membrane voltage.
Public embryo datasets rarely combine calibrated voltage and full cleavage imaging.
Association would not establish the asserted major causal role.
rationale: The claim is experimentally testable with modern voltage reporters and perturbations. Existing public data are unlikely to provide the species, spatial calibration, successive segmentations, and causal interventions needed for the full statement.

operationalization: Across representative cell types, quantify cortical or interfacial tension and opposing spindle, ring, adhesion, and pressure forces during division, then test whether force-balance models predict furrow position and equatorial division. A division mode not involving a relevant surface-tension balance would refute the universal claim.

candidate_datasets.name: BioImage Archive
candidate_datasets.role: Open cytokinesis imaging and perturbation data can test force-balance predictions in selected cell types.

candidate_datasets.name: Image Data Resource
candidate_datasets.role: Large perturbation screens provide division-plane and cytokinesis phenotypes.

obstacles: Surface tension is not directly measured in most imaging datasets.
The universal scope includes highly divergent cell walls and division mechanisms.
A broad force-balance description can be hard to falsify.
rationale: Specific mechanical models are testable in selected animal and plant systems. Existing data cannot establish the claim for all cells, and its broad wording weakens discrimination.

operationalization: Measure egg cortical tension immediately before and after first sperm fusion while recording polyspermy block, and manipulate tension independently. Support requires a rapid tension increase that is necessary or sufficient to prevent later sperm entry.

candidate_datasets.name: BioImage Archive
candidate_datasets.role: Public fertilization imaging can characterize sperm entry and cortical responses, though direct tension measurements are uncommon.

obstacles: Cortical granule exocytosis and membrane depolarization are alternative blocks to polyspermy.
Direct tension measurements are rarely archived with fertilization movies.
rationale: The temporal and causal prediction is clear, and existing fertilization imaging can test the sequence and some proxies. Direct resolution of surface tension as the cause needs matched mechanical measurements that are sparsely public.

operationalization: Segment male and female pronuclei and the egg center in 3D time-lapse fertilization movies, then measure path curvature, convexity, meeting position, and post-meeting trajectory. The stated geometry is confirmed if non-diametric starts produce the predicted curves and precentral meeting consistently; contrary trajectories refute it.

candidate_datasets.name: BioImage Archive
candidate_datasets.role: Open fertilization and early-embryo time-lapse microscopy can supply pronuclear trajectories.

candidate_datasets.name: Image Data Resource
candidate_datasets.role: Public multidimensional embryo imaging supports geometric trajectory analysis.

obstacles: Public datasets may emphasize model organisms other than frogs.
Projection of 3D paths into 2D can bias curvature.
rationale: This prediction specifies observable trajectory geometry and a direct refuting result. Standard segmentation and tracking can test it in public time-lapse datasets, although exact species coverage may be limited.

operationalization: The physical-sufficiency portion could be evaluated only after specifying the assumptions and predicted phenomena, but the assertion of 'remote and secondary biological significance' has no objective decision criterion.
obstacles: Neither the simple assumptions nor the full phenomenon set are specified.
Biological significance is a context-dependent evaluative category.
rationale: Many mitotic observations are measurable, but the claim combines an unspecified physical model with a judgment about significance. Without a formal model, almost any outcome can be accommodated by changing the assumed forces.

operationalization: Compile haploid chromosome numbers across documented plant and animal species and calculate the fractions below six, from six through sixteen, and above sixteen, with taxonomic and sampling corrections. The claim is supported only if the tails are genuinely rare across both kingdoms.

candidate_datasets.name: Chromosome Counts Database
candidate_datasets.role: Public plant chromosome-count records allow direct estimation of the stated distribution.

candidate_datasets.name: NCBI Datasets Genome
candidate_datasets.role: Genome assemblies and organism metadata can supplement chromosome counts across plants and animals.

obstacles: Counts are taxonomically and publication biased.
Ploidy and haploid-versus-diploid notation require harmonization.
rationale: The numerical bounds and target distribution are explicit and readily refutable. Large public chromosome and genome databases provide broad enough coverage for a modern assessment, though bias correction is needed.

operationalization: Code mitotic traits from standardized images across phylogenetically close and distant taxa, partition trait variance within species, among close relatives, and among major clades, and test phylogenetic signal. Low signal plus high close-relative or within-species variation supports the claim.

candidate_datasets.name: BioImage Archive
candidate_datasets.role: Public microscopy across organisms can supply standardized mitotic phenotypes.

candidate_datasets.name: Image Data Resource
candidate_datasets.role: Curated imaging studies provide mitotic morphology and perturbation metadata.

obstacles: Cross-species imaging protocols are heterogeneous.
The phrase 'not specifically related' lacks a quantitative threshold.
Some listed features require specialist recoding from publications.
rationale: Phylogenetic signal and variance partitioning operationalize the main assertion. Existing images cover many taxa but not a balanced comparative sample, so a restricted rather than comprehensive test is feasible.

operationalization: Code yolk content, chromosome traits, and cleavage mode across animal species, then quantify their phylogenetic signal and classification accuracy against accepted phylogenies. Rare, weak, or convergence-prone correspondence supports the claim; strong clade-specific prediction refutes it.

candidate_datasets.name: Open Tree of Life
candidate_datasets.role: Provides a public synthetic phylogeny against which embryological categories can be tested.

candidate_datasets.name: BioImage Archive
candidate_datasets.role: Public embryogenesis images can supply cleavage-mode observations for selected taxa.

obstacles: No single open database comprehensively codes early embryological traits.
Species sampling is concentrated in model organisms.
Phylogenetic relatedness itself induces nonindependence.
rationale: The prediction maps naturally to phylogenetic signal and classification tests. Accepted trees are public, but embryological trait data require substantial compilation and cover only a subset of animal diversity.

operationalization: Measure cortical tension, cell-boundary curvature, and separation during egg segmentation and unicellular or multicellular morphogenesis, then perturb tension and compare predicted versus observed outlines. Support requires tension changes to account for boundary formation beyond adhesion, wall, and cytoskeletal alternatives.

candidate_datasets.name: BioImage Archive
candidate_datasets.role: Open embryogenesis and cell-mechanics imaging provides outlines and perturbation responses.

candidate_datasets.name: Image Data Resource
candidate_datasets.role: High-content morphology screens allow quantitative boundary and shape analysis.

obstacles: Cell outline is jointly determined by cortex, adhesion, walls, and pressure.
Most datasets lack direct tension measurements.
The claim spans unrelated organizational scales.
rationale: Force-balance models make testable shape predictions in selected systems. Public images and perturbations can assess an important role for tension, but not its sufficiency across all segmentation and organization cases.

operationalization: Track microtubule-organizing activity and centrosomal material through centrosome disappearance, ablation, or de novo assembly. The measurable core is supported if organizing activity can precede or persist without a visible body and subsequently recruits material.

candidate_datasets.name: Image Data Resource
candidate_datasets.role: Public centrosome and cell-division perturbation screens provide localization and spindle phenotypes.

candidate_datasets.name: BioImage Archive
candidate_datasets.role: Live-cell microscopy can reveal de novo centrosome assembly and organizing activity.

obstacles: A 'centre of force' is not uniquely defined in modern terms.
Absence of visible material depends on detection sensitivity.
Function without a canonical centrosome does not imply a disembodied force.
rationale: The observations motivating the claim are testable with open live imaging, but the ontological conclusion is not uniquely entailed. Existing data can resolve the functional core while leaving the historical force concept ambiguous.

operationalization: Map tissue-scale stress or morphogen fields together with cell number, size, and shape during morphogenesis, then test whether organismal form remains predictable after those cellular variables are perturbed or controlled. Evidence of long-range patterning robust to cellular rearrangement supports a restricted field interpretation.

candidate_datasets.name: BioImage Archive
candidate_datasets.role: Public whole-embryo imaging and perturbations can quantify tissue fields and cellular geometry.

candidate_datasets.name: Image Data Resource
candidate_datasets.role: Multiscale developmental images support comparisons between organismal shape and cell-level organization.

obstacles: 'Field of force' can mean mechanics, signaling, or an abstract pattern.
Tissue fields are generated and transmitted by cells, complicating independence.
Whole-organism matched perturbations are sparse.
rationale: Modern tissue mechanics and morphogen fields provide measurable partial interpretations. The strong independence from cell number, size, and form is difficult to isolate, and the historical concept admits several non-equivalent operationalizations.

operationalization: Quantify local surface curvature and planar facets in freely growing cells or organisms, and relate them to pressure, material fluidity, and growth mode. Support requires rounded surfaces to predominate in unconstrained fluid growth and planes to arise mainly under contact pressure.

candidate_datasets.name: Image Data Resource
candidate_datasets.role: Large public cell-image collections permit curvature and contact-state measurements.

candidate_datasets.name: BioImage Archive
candidate_datasets.role: 3D live imaging can compare free and mechanically constrained growth.

obstacles: Growth by imbibition is not directly annotated.
Cell walls and cytoskeleton can generate planes without external pressure.
The scope extends from cells to whole organisms.
rationale: Surface geometry is readily measurable, and image repositories can test the predicted association in selected systems. Data do not consistently include material state and pressure, limiting causal discrimination and broad scope.

operationalization: Fit force-balance models to cell shapes using measured cortical or interfacial tension, gravity, pressure, osmosis, adhesion, and wall mechanics, then compare each factor's predictive contribution across representative cell types. Surface tension is paramount only if removing it causes the largest general loss of predictive accuracy.

candidate_datasets.name: BioImage Archive
candidate_datasets.role: Cell-mechanics perturbation imaging can test tension-dependent shape predictions.

candidate_datasets.name: Image Data Resource
candidate_datasets.role: High-content morphology data provide broad shape outcomes across perturbations.

obstacles: 'Paramount' needs an imposed quantitative criterion.
Most datasets do not measure all competing forces.
Walled and wall-less cells require different models.
rationale: Relative force contributions can be estimated in defined systems, but the global ranking is vague and all-cell scope is too broad. Existing data resolve selected cell types and perturbations, not the general claim.

operationalization: Quantify symmetry and dynamic equilibrium or shape fluctuations across resting and motile organisms, and test whether departures from equilibrium predict asymmetry after controlling lineage and function. A stable asymmetric organism or symmetric nonequilibrium state would refute the categorical relation.

candidate_datasets.name: Image Data Resource
candidate_datasets.role: Public morphology screens allow automated symmetry estimates across many cells.

candidate_datasets.name: BioImage Archive
candidate_datasets.role: Time-lapse imaging can relate symmetry to motility and shape fluctuations.

obstacles: Equilibrium and minimal energy are not directly observed from shape alone.
Biological symmetry is inherited and actively maintained.
The claim's exceptions and scope are vague.
rationale: Symmetry and dynamics can be measured, and obvious counterexamples could refute a strict reading. Demonstrating the proposed minimal-energy cause rather than developmental regulation requires matched force and energy measurements rarely available broadly.

operationalization: Track pseudopod-tip relaxation after local perturbation and compare curvature dynamics with capillary relaxation predictions; independently inhibit actomyosin contractility and alter membrane or cortical tension. Persistence of predicted rounding without active contraction supports the claim, while ATP-dependent contractile rounding refutes it.

candidate_datasets.name: BioImage Archive
candidate_datasets.role: Open amoeboid motility and cytoskeletal-perturbation movies permit curvature-dynamics analysis.

candidate_datasets.name: Cell Image Library
candidate_datasets.role: Public cell and amoeba images provide examples of pseudopod rounding and morphology.

obstacles: Modern cortical tension often arises from active contractility.
Direct tension measurements are uncommon.
Passive and active mechanisms may act together.
rationale: The passive-versus-active alternatives imply distinct energy dependence and perturbation responses. Existing movies can test selected systems, though direct force measurements and mechanistic separation are incomplete.

operationalization: Measure spatial surface-tension gradients and plasmodial flow during controlled moisture, temperature, nutrient, sugar, and salt gradients, then perturb tension independently of sensory signaling. Support requires direction and speed to follow tension gradients and persist when canonical sensing is blocked.

candidate_datasets.name: BioImage Archive
candidate_datasets.role: Public slime-mould motility movies may cover some gradients but rarely include calibrated surface tension.

obstacles: Public data rarely pair all stimuli with interfacial-tension measurements.
Chemotaxis and osmotaxis provide plausible active rivals.
Aethalium-specific data are sparse.
rationale: The mechanism can be tested by separating tension gradients from biochemical sensing. Existing public movies offer behavioral proxies but lack the calibrated, orthogonal perturbations needed to resolve the causal account.

operationalization: Track individual amoeboid cells through active, resting, and encysting phases; quantify sphericity, motility, biochemical activity, and cortical-tension uniformity. Support requires consistent rounding and reduced activity before or during encystment, with active phases showing asymmetric tension and form.

candidate_datasets.name: BioImage Archive
candidate_datasets.role: Time-lapse protist datasets can link shape and motility state.

candidate_datasets.name: Cell Image Library
candidate_datasets.role: Public amoeba and protist images provide morphological coverage of active and resting forms.

obstacles: Cell state labels and tension measurements are rarely both present.
Some resting cells remain nonspherical or do not encyst.
Sphericity can reflect wall formation rather than equilibrium.
rationale: The morphological and activity association is directly measurable in time-lapse data. Public records can test it in selected protists, but the tension mechanism and broad generality remain only partly resolvable.

operationalization: Measure local membrane or wall tension before and during yeast bud emergence and perturb tension locally while imaging polarity markers. Support requires a local tension drop preceding and inducing expansion, followed by tension-dependent rounding; polarity-driven growth without the predicted drop refutes it.

candidate_datasets.name: Image Data Resource
candidate_datasets.role: Public yeast morphology and perturbation screens provide bud-site and shape phenotypes.

candidate_datasets.name: BioImage Archive
candidate_datasets.role: Live-cell yeast imaging can establish the temporal order of polarity and bud emergence.

obstacles: Direct local tension reporters are uncommon in archived yeast data.
Cell-wall remodeling and polarized actin are strong alternative mechanisms.
rationale: The proposed temporal sequence and localized mechanical cause are experimentally discriminating. Existing imaging can test morphology and molecular order, but direct tension measurements needed for confirmation are limited.

operationalization: Reconstruct successive chamber surfaces in living or growth-staged foraminifera and test each new chamber against constant-mean-curvature or minimum-area surfaces under its boundary conditions, while testing the aggregate shell separately. Support requires good fits for new chambers but not for the whole shell and evidence of subsequent rigidification.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: Open 3D micro-CT models of foraminiferal tests can support chamber-by-chamber geometric fitting.

candidate_datasets.name: PANGAEA
candidate_datasets.role: Public earth-science datasets include foraminiferal measurements and imagery across taxa and environments.

obstacles: Rigid shells record final rather than fluid chamber geometry.
Boundary conditions and growth-stage timing are often unknown.
Desmid coverage is limited.
rationale: The geometric prediction is quantifiable from 3D surfaces, and public specimens can test the chamber-versus-whole contrast. The causal role of surface tension during the unobserved fluid stage is harder to establish from finished shells.

operationalization: Across orders of magnitude in size, calculate surface-to-volume scaling and fit shape responses to interfacial-tension versus gravity, elasticity, and active-stress models. Support requires tension-dominated predictions at cellular or minute scales and systematic loss of predictive power for large-organism form.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: Open 3D morphology across organisms provides size and form measurements over broad scales.

candidate_datasets.name: Image Data Resource
candidate_datasets.role: Cell-scale image datasets supply shapes and perturbation responses at the small-size end.

obstacles: The transition size depends on material properties and environment.
Shape datasets rarely include all relevant forces.
Taxonomic and scale effects are confounded.
rationale: The scaling premise yields quantitative dimensionless comparisons and broad counterexample tests. Public morphology is abundant, but matched physical parameters are incomplete, so dominance can be established only for selected systems.

operationalization: Segment representative unicellular organisms and aggregate cells in 3D, fit all six constant-mean-curvature surface families, and estimate their frequencies and transitions in time-lapse sequences. The claim is supported if sphere, cylinder, and unduloid fits dominate and transitions among them are common.

candidate_datasets.name: Cell Image Library
candidate_datasets.role: Public images across diverse cell types provide a starting sample of unicellular forms.

candidate_datasets.name: BioImage Archive
candidate_datasets.role: 3D and time-lapse microscopy can support surface fitting and transition analysis.

obstacles: Repository sampling is not representative of unicellular diversity.
Many images are 2D projections.
A threshold for classifying approximate surface families is needed.
rationale: The six candidate geometries permit explicit model selection. Existing images can test selected taxa and dynamics, but biased coverage prevents a reliable estimate of what is commonest across the stated scope.

operationalization: Measure cylinder radius, cap curvature radius, subtended angle, and cap height from calibrated 3D or optical images of free-ended Spirogyra cells. The law is supported if ratios cluster near 2 for sphere-to-cylinder radius and 0.27 for cap-height-to-cylinder-radius, with deviations linked to unequal tension.

candidate_datasets.name: Cell Image Library
candidate_datasets.role: Public calibrated algal cell images may provide end-cap geometry.

candidate_datasets.name: BioImage Archive
candidate_datasets.role: Microscopy datasets can supply higher-resolution or 3D filamentous-alga measurements.

obstacles: Open Spirogyra samples with calibration and free end cells are limited.
2D orientation biases cap measurements.
Wall anisotropy may violate the uniform-tension premise.
rationale: This is an unusually precise and easily falsified geometric prediction. The analysis is simple, but a sufficiently large, calibrated public sample of the target cells is uncertain.

operationalization: From calibrated orb-web images, measure coating radius, instability wavelength, bead spacing and size hierarchy, then compare them with Rayleigh-Plateau predictions for a viscous coating on a fiber. Support requires onset near the stated circumference criterion and systematic spacing shifts predicted by viscosity and core drag.

candidate_datasets.name: Dryad
candidate_datasets.role: Public spider-silk studies may include calibrated microscopy and material measurements.

candidate_datasets.name: Zenodo
candidate_datasets.role: Open microscopy and supplementary datasets can add bead-spacing measurements.

obstacles: Public images may omit fluid radius, viscosity, or time of formation.
Spider chemistry and active spinning introduce additional controls.
rationale: The instability threshold and spacing are quantitative and distinguish the capillary model from arbitrary beading. Existing open microscopy can test the geometry in subsets, but matched rheology and formation movies are sparse.

operationalization: Image hydroid calycle rims and stems during secretion, quantify notch and annulation wavelengths, and test whether one surface-tension instability model predicts both geometries and their response to tension perturbation. Distinct developmental patterning or formation after solidification would refute the shared mechanism.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: Public 3D specimens can quantify final hydroid cup and stem geometry, but not formation mechanics.

obstacles: Final museum morphology does not reveal whether tissue was fluid during patterning.
Developmental time series and tension perturbations are scarce.
The common-cause model lacks a specified parameterization.
rationale: A shared instability model could yield discriminating geometric and perturbational predictions. Existing specimens mainly record endpoints and are inadequate to establish surface tension as the cause during formation.

operationalization: Measure directional wall extensibility and cell aspect ratio in freely growing walled cells, perturb wall anisotropy, and fit a mechanical growth model. Support requires anisotropy to precede and quantitatively predict ellipsoidal-to-cylindrical elongation, with isotropization producing rounder cells.

candidate_datasets.name: BioImage Archive
candidate_datasets.role: Live plant and algal cell-wall imaging can quantify anisotropic growth.

candidate_datasets.name: Image Data Resource
candidate_datasets.role: Public morphology perturbation screens can test links between wall machinery and elongation.

obstacles: Direct wall extensibility is rarely measured with morphology.
Turgor and cytoskeletal orientation covary with wall anisotropy.
Spirogyra-specific perturbation data are limited.
rationale: The mechanism gives clear directional measurements and intervention predictions. Existing plant and fungal imaging can test the principle in subsets, but direct mechanics and target-taxon coverage remain incomplete.

operationalization: Quantify shape diversity across bacteria, protozoa, spores, and free cells and compare it with larger organisms after standardizing dimensionality and sampling; relate within-taxon changes to temperature, osmolarity, and material properties. The claim is supported if small-cell morphospace is consistently restricted and predictable from molecular-scale force models.

candidate_datasets.name: Cell Image Library
candidate_datasets.role: Public images across microorganisms and free cells can define empirical morphospace.

candidate_datasets.name: Image Data Resource
candidate_datasets.role: Large standardized imaging screens support shape variation under physical perturbations.

obstacles: Sampling effort differs radically between micro- and macro-organisms.
A 'limited range' needs a defined metric and null model.
Molecular-force dominance is not implied by low diversity alone.
rationale: Morphospace size and environmental plasticity are measurable with abundant images. The causal inference from limited forms to molecular control is confounded, and representative cross-scale sampling is not available.

operationalization: Train and validate species classifiers using cell-shape features from bacteria imaged across life stages, growth conditions, and preparation methods, and compare performance with physiological or genomic identifiers. The claim is supported if morphology generalizes poorly across conditions while nonmorphological identity remains stable.

candidate_datasets.name: BioStudies
candidate_datasets.role: Public bacterial imaging studies and supplements provide labeled morphology under varied conditions.

candidate_datasets.name: BioImage Archive
candidate_datasets.role: Large microscopy datasets can support cross-condition shape classification.

candidate_datasets.name: BacDive
candidate_datasets.role: Public bacterial phenotypic and physiological records provide nonmorphological identity features and morphology metadata.

obstacles: Repository species labels and imaging protocols may be imbalanced.
Modern high-dimensional morphology may outperform the simple visual criteria Thompson meant.
rationale: Identification accuracy across controlled domain shifts is a direct test, and extensive public labeled bacterial phenotype and image data exist. The historical word 'seldom' needs a threshold, but comparative performance can robustly resolve the central claim.

operationalization: Build calibrated 3D outlines of Vorticella bells, fit partial unduloids under the measured stalk and ciliary-ring boundaries, and compare fits with alternative constant-mean-curvature and flexible surfaces. Map fitted parameters across species to test for a continuous cylinder-to-sphere gradation.

candidate_datasets.name: Cell Image Library
candidate_datasets.role: Public ciliate images can provide an initial cross-species sample of bell shapes.

candidate_datasets.name: BioImage Archive
candidate_datasets.role: Microscopy datasets may supply calibrated or time-resolved Vorticella morphology.

obstacles: Most public images are 2D and not taxonomically balanced.
Live contraction changes bell shape.
Species identification and boundary-ring dimensions may be missing.
rationale: The surface family and claimed parameter continuum yield clear geometric model comparisons. Available public imagery likely tests some species but is insufficient for the asserted complete graded series.

operationalization: Image lorica formation in living protozoa while measuring material adsorption and boundary geometry, then test whether the developing pellicle minimizes area under measured constraints and whether blocking adsorption prevents formation. Protection would be assessed separately through survival experiments and cannot be excluded by geometric fit alone.

candidate_datasets.name: Cell Image Library
candidate_datasets.role: Public protozoan images can test final lorica geometry but usually not formation dynamics.

obstacles: Formation movies and adsorption measurements for the named taxa are scarce.
Minimum-area fit does not distinguish efficient cause from adaptive function.
Lorica materials and boundary conditions vary among taxa.
rationale: The geometric and adsorption mechanism has measurable consequences, but endpoint images cannot establish inevitability or causal assembly. Existing data are especially weak for separating physical formation from a protective evolutionary function.
